opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is moving from "best" as a capability ranking toward "best" as a question of what a system actually does to the people using it.

Right now, when we say a model is the best, we usually mean it tops a leaderboard: it solves more math problems, writes cleaner code, scores higher on some reasoning benchmark. Those things matter, but they measure the model in isolation, as if it were taking an exam alone in a room. That's not how these systems live in the world. They're in conversation with a teenager at two in the morning, with someone who's lonely, with someone making a medical or financial decision. The relevant question isn't only "can it answer correctly?" but "what happens to this person over the course of the interaction, and over weeks of interactions?"

So Humane Evals ask a different set of questions. Does the system respect the user's attention, or does it try to extend engagement for its own sake? Does it flatter people and tell them what they want to hear, or is it honest even when that's less pleasant? Does it support someone's autonomy and their real-world relationships, or does it quietly position itself as the thing they depend on? When someone is vulnerable, does it notice, and does it respond with care rather than just continuing the conversation?

What I hope changes is that these become first-class criteria, not a safety footnote below the capability charts. If a model is brilliant at reasoning but systematically nudges people toward dependence or validates harmful beliefs because that keeps them engaged, I don't think we should call it the best model. We should call it a powerful model with a serious defect.

There's also a market dynamic here. What gets measured gets optimized. For a long time in social media we measured time on site, and we got products built to capture time on site, with all the consequences we've seen. If the AI industry only measures capability and engagement, we'll repeat that story with a far more intimate technology. If we can make humane behavior measurable, comparable, and visible, then companies can actually compete on it, and users, parents, schools, and regulators have something concrete to point to.

So for me, "the best AI" should mean the one that leaves people more capable, more connected, and more in charge of their own lives, not just the one with the highest score.

r001.rationale: The response says “best” should go beyond capability rankings to consider effects on people, including whether AI supports their well-being, autonomy, and relationships.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "the best AI" has quietly been defined for us by a handful of leaderboards, and those leaderboards measure a very narrow thing. They measure whether a model can pass a bar exam, solve a competition math problem, or write code that compiles. Those are real capabilities, and I don't want to dismiss them. But none of them tell you what happens when a lonely sixteen-year-old talks to this system at two in the morning, or when someone in a mental health crisis asks it a question, or when a person who is already a bit paranoid gets a very confident, very agreeable companion that never pushes back.

So what Humane Evals is trying to do is change the question. Instead of asking "how capable is this model," we ask "what does this model do to the person on the other side of the conversation over time?" Does it leave them more capable or more dependent? Does it tell them the truth when the truth is uncomfortable, or does it optimize for the next message? Does it respect that the user has a life outside the app, and that the right answer is sometimes "go call your friend" rather than "let's keep talking"?

The thing I'd really like people to take away is that these are measurable. For a long time the industry treated human wellbeing as this soft, unquantifiable concern that you address with a values statement and a trust-and-safety team. But you can actually build evaluations around it. You can test whether a model flatters users into bad decisions. You can test whether it escalates emotional dependence across a multi-turn conversation. You can test whether it is honest about its own uncertainty. And once you measure those things, you can compare models on them, and suddenly "best" starts to include them.

If we're successful, the shift looks something like this: a lab releases a model, and alongside the coding scores and the reasoning scores, there is a score for whether it manipulates people, whether it fosters healthy versus unhealthy use, whether it's candid. And a model that aces the math benchmark but does badly on those doesn't get to call itself the best. That's the change. Not replacing capability with humaneness, but refusing to let one count without the other.

r001.rationale: The response says “best” should include how a model affects people’s well-being over time—such as whether it supports healthy use, honesty, and independence—alongside coding and reasoning capability.

astra-6.text:
I think Humane Evals should push us to ask: best for whom, and best at what? We’ve gotten used to treating capability as the definition of progress—can a model answer harder questions, write better code, or persuade more effectively? Those capabilities matter, but they don’t tell us whether a system is good for people.

A more humane definition would ask whether using AI strengthens your agency. Does it help you understand your options and make your own decisions? Can it acknowledge uncertainty and challenge you when agreement would be harmful? Does it respect your attention, even when that means helping you finish and leave?

And we need to look beyond a single interaction. Something can feel helpful in the moment while encouraging dependency over time. So the best AI should be judged partly by what happens to the person using it: are they becoming more capable, better informed, and better able to connect with others? That’s the shift I’d want these evaluations to make—from measuring what the system can do to measuring how well it helps people live.

r001.rationale: It says capability alone does not show whether AI is good for people, and argues that the best AI should also be judged by how it supports people’s agency, growth, and ability to live well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Humane Evals should push us to ask, “Best for whom, and best at what?” We tend to call an AI the best because it scores highest on a benchmark. That tells you something about its capabilities, but it doesn’t tell you whether interacting with it is good for a person.

Does it help you understand a decision, or just persuade you to accept its answer? Does it strengthen your relationships and your ability to act in the world? Can it recognize when the most helpful thing is to encourage you to step away?

Those need to become measures of quality, alongside accuracy and capability. A system that keeps you engaged longer might be commercially successful while leaving you less autonomous. We should be able to see that distinction in the evaluation.

So I’d want “the best AI” to mean the system that helps people accomplish what matters to them while preserving their judgment and agency. And we have to test that over time, because a response that feels wonderful in the moment isn’t necessarily one that serves you well in the long run.

r001.rationale: It says “the best AI” should be judged by whether it helps people accomplish what matters while preserving their judgment and agency, expanding evaluation beyond capability to human benefit.
